column4: The section's returned, faulty coin meets a Qur'anic dinar entrusted to one who returns it, while another refuses its return; the ayah makes trust and coin-value meet concretely.
The section's full-weight dinar and just judgment meet the placed balance, الْمِيزَانُ; this verse introduces the measure whose justice the next ayat specify.
The section's coin that fails its standard meets the command not to transgress the balance, الْمِيزَانِ; the measure is a moral boundary as well as a physical one.
The section's calibrated dinar and just verdict meet the command to establish weight in justice, الْوَزْنَ بِالْقِسْطِ; the ayah joins accurate measure to fairness.
The section's sarraf tests a coin's weight and rejects the faulty one; Shuʿayb commands full measure and weight and forbids depriving people, وَزِنُوا بِالْقِسْطَاسِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ.
The section's calibrated coin meets Shuʿayb's instruction to give full measure and weight justly, أَوْفُوا الْمِكْيَالَ وَالْمِيزَانَ بِالْقِسْطِ; the surrounding warning makes fraud consequential.
The section's rejected underweight coin meets the repeated command to complete measure and weight and not diminish people's goods; the verse names the exact market wrong behind the image.
The section's full-weight dinar and balanced judgment meet the instruction to fill the measure and weigh with the straight balance, الْقِسْطَاسِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ.
The section's defective coin returned at the assayer's bench meets the command to complete the measure and not cause loss, أَوْفُوا الْكَيْلَ وَلَا تَكُونُوا مِنَ الْمُخْسِرِينَ.
The section's coin must be properly calibrated; this continuation commands weighing with the even balance, وَزِنُوا بِالْقِسْطَاسِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ.
The section's rejected false coin corresponds to Shuʿayb's warning not to deprive people of their due or spread corruption; the verse supplies the ethical result of crooked measure.
The section's full-weight coin and fair judgment meet the command to complete measure and weight in justice, بِالْقِسْطِ; the verse makes honest measure a divine rule.
The section's counterfeit, returned by the assayer, meets the woe pronounced on those who give short measure, الْمُطَفِّفِينَ; this is the closest direct image of defective weighing.
The section's weighing bench meets the act of taking a full measure for oneself, اكْتَالُوا عَلَى النَّاسِ; this verse begins the imbalance the following verse reverses.
The section's true-weight coin opposes giving others less when measuring or weighing, يُخْسِرُونَ; the ayah exposes the same standard applied differently to self and neighbor.

The section's measure-and-verdict meeting continues into the question whether the short-measurers expect to be raised; this verse contributes the link between market deceit and the afterlife reckoning.
The section's wage and judgment scenes converge in the great day named here, يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ; this ayah completes the question begun at 83:4 before people stand.
The section explicitly brings in the root ق و م through the standing of people before the Judge; this ayah says يَوْمَ يَقُومُ النَّاسُ لِرَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ.
The section's full-weight coin and just judgment meet scales set for Resurrection, الْمَوَازِينَ الْقِسْطَ; no soul is wronged even by a mustard seed.
The section's sound work weighed for reward meets the true weighing on that Day, فَمَن ثَقُلَتْ مَوَازِينُهُ; deeds receive an actual measure.
The section's sound deed that holds its value is set against the light scale and loss here; this ayah states the contrary outcome of misweighted deeds.
The section's wages and the just balance meet those whose scales are heavy, الْمَوَازِينُ; this ayah makes the weight of a life's work decisive.
The section's sound work and uncut reward meet the opposite case: light scales mean loss of self; the ayah gives the boundary to the promised outcome.
The section's fitting deed and full-value wage meet the heavy scales, ثَقُلَتْ مَوَازِينُهُ; the image of measured value becomes the criterion for a good life.
The section's lasting wage meets the pleasing life that follows heavy scales; this verse names what the successful measure yields.
The section's sound work meets the explicit opposite of a light balance, خَفَّتْ مَوَازِينُهُ; this verse starts the contrary fate to the enduring wage.
The section's descent and its mention of Hell's lowest level meet the abyss, هَاوِيَةٌ, assigned to the light-scaled; this verse completes that reversal.
The section's returned counterfeit and just ruling meet the command to restore trusts and judge among people with justice, بِالْعَدْلِ; both benches depend on a fair standard.
The section's upright human, sound measure, and just judge meet the command to stand firm for God as witnesses in justice, كُونُوا قَوَّامِينَ لِلَّهِ شُهَدَاءَ بِالْقِسْطِ.
The section's root ق و م links bodily uprightness with measured justice; this verse commands people to stand persistently for justice even against themselves or kin.
The section's dictionary family for أَجْر includes a bone that heals crookedly; this verse asks whether human bones will be gathered after death, making the bone image bodily and eschatological.
The section's bone-straightening sense meets God's ability to proportion even fingertips, بَنَانَهُ; the verse shows precise restoration rather than a crooked repair.
The section's dictionary form for أَجْر includes a bone set crooked; this ayah raises the challenge of reviving decayed bones and thus makes the lexical bone image literal.
The section's straightening and creation meeting is answered by the One who made bones the first time; this neighboring verse grounds restoration in original creation.
The section explicitly links رَدَدْنَاهُ to life's return to its frailest age; this ayah names womb stages, that age, dead soil revived, and resurrection as evidence for the Hour.
The section notes that أَسْفَل also names Hell's lowest depth; this verse places hypocrites in the lowest level, a specific infernal counterpart to the human's fall.
The section's spatial and temporal dictionary senses of رَدَّ meet creation from earth, return into it, and emergence from it again, مِنْهَا نُخْرِجُكُمْ تَارَةً أُخْرَى.
The section says the fifth verse's رَدّ and the eighth verse's judgment meet; here people are returned to their true master and الحكم is His, فَرُدُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ مَوْلَاهُمُ الْحَقِّ.
The section's return from life's descent meets the promise that all return to God, إِلَيْهِ مَرْجِعُكُمْ جَمِيعًا; the verse ties that return to creation begun and repeated.
The section's return after human creation meets the statement that God begins creation, repeats it, and to Him people return, ثُمَّ إِلَيْهِ تُرْجَعُونَ.
The section's best creation followed by return meets God's ability to originate creation and repeat it; this verse grounds the rise after descent in the Creator's power.
The section's ending life, divine judgment, and return meet the statement that all things perish but God's face, الحكم belongs to Him, and people return to Him.
The section's fall through life's stages and return to judgment meet the sequence of being lifeless, revived, made to die, revived again, then returned to God.
The section's root ر د د includes turning back; at death the wrongdoer asks to be sent back to do right, رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ, linking return with unfinished work.
The section's return and uncut-work meeting meets the barrier until resurrection; this neighbor explains why the requested return cannot supply a second chance before judgment.
The section's dictionary family for بَلَد includes ground and buried bodies; this ayah begins with the earth shaken at the Resurrection, when the hidden dead are about to emerge.
The section's ground, grave, and bodily descent meet the earth casting out its burdens, أَثْقَالَهَا; this neighbor makes the buried bodies part of the reckoning scene.
The section's return before judgment meets people emerging in separate groups to be shown their deeds; the ayah links the earth's release to individual accounting.
The section's calibrated worth and lasting wage meet even an atom's weight of good being seen, مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا; no deed is too small to count.
The section's sound work and reward meet the matching atom's weight of evil being seen; this neighbor completes the balanced accounting of 99:7.
The section's life ending and return meet the statement that every soul tastes death and then returns to God; mortality does not cancel the final reckoning.
The section's return to the weakest age meets the sequence from dust and a drop through maturity and old age; the verse makes death before the appointed term part of that same measure.
The section's human fashioned in best proportion meets the beginning of human creation from an extract of clay, سُلَالَةٍ مِّن طِينٍ.
The section's upright body has a staged beginning; this next verse places the human drop in a secure resting place, قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ.
The section's soundly fashioned body meets the stages ending in bones clothed with flesh and then a further creation; it gives bodily substance to its takwim image.
The section's uncut reward meets the immediate reminder that humans die after their bodily formation; the verse marks the interruption that the next verse's resurrection answers.
The section's return and standing before judgment meet the promise that people will be raised on the Day of Resurrection; this neighbor completes the life-stage sequence.
The section's human made in best proportion meets the question of what material he was created from; the following verses trace the making that precedes death and reawakening.
The section's measured human formation meets creation from a drop and its apportionment, فَقَدَّرَهُ; this verse names the fitting of human life.
The section's course from upright creation toward descent meets the way made easy for human life; the next verses continue through death and reawakening.
The section's descent and the life that ends meet the statement that God causes the human to die and be buried, فَأَقْبَرَهُ.
The section's return and standing meet the promise that when God wills He will raise the buried human, أَنْشَرَهُ; this completes the neighboring death sequence.
The section's crafted human form meets the origin as a drop of emitted fluid; this verse begins the same creation-to-resurrection argument.
The section's proportioned body meets the formation of a clot into a fashioned human, فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّى; the verse gives the process behind the image.
The section's completed human form meets the creation of the two sexes from that fashioned beginning; the verse extends the body's measured making.
The section's created human who may fall is asked whether the Creator can revive the dead; this neighbor turns formation directly toward return.
The section's best-proportioned human meets God's making of all things good and the start of human creation from clay; the verse joins creation to fitness.
The section's human form meets the continuation from clay into progeny from a humble fluid; this neighbor specifies the bodily sequence.
The section's upright, fitted person meets the verse saying He fashioned the human and breathed of His spirit into him; this is the closest creation-side counterpart.
The section's أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيم is matched by God shaping people and making their forms good, صَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ; provision and lordship complete the setting.
The section's best form meets the statement that God created and shaped people well, وَصَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ; this verse also points toward the return.
The section's creation and straightening meeting recalls God's creation and forming of humanity before the command to bow; the verse makes the form a setting for moral response.
The section's fitting and straightening image meets the proportioned soul, سَوَّاهَا; this ayah makes formation the premise for the moral alternatives in the next verses.
The section's sound work versus crookedness meets the soul made to recognize its wickedness and piety; this neighbor names the moral measure of what follows.
The section's صالحات and enduring wage meet success through purifying the soul, قَدْ أَفْلَحَ مَن زَكَّاهَا; this is the positive course after formation.
The section's fall to the lowest is illuminated by the soul's failure when buried in corruption, وَقَدْ خَابَ مَن دَسَّاهَا; the neighbor states formation's contrary outcome.
The section's work judged for an uncut wage meets the reason God created death and life: to test who is best in deed, أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا.
The section names this exact meeting: the command to set the face toward religion, the creation/fıṭra, and the root ق و م in الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ occur together here.
The section's human made in best proportion meets the question of who created, proportioned, and balanced the person, خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّاكَ فَعَدَلَكَ; this starts the form-to-religion sequence.
The section's human form meets God's composition into whatever form He willed, فِي أَيِّ صُورَةٍ مَّا شَاءَ رَكَّبَكَ; the verse completes the bodily sequence before denial of judgment.
The section places creation and form before denial of dīn; this ayah says people deny the Recompense, بِالدِّينِ, immediately after 82:7–8's forming.
The section distinguishes God's real creation from humanly fabricated falsehood; this ayah uses تَخْلُقُونَ إِفْكًا for the latter and turns directly to God as provider.
The section says رَدّ has the dictionary sense of turning back from religion; this ayah names turning back from dīn and losing one's works, a precise religious reversal.
The section's dictionary sense of رَدّ as apostasy meets the question who would turn back from religion; the verse contrasts apostasy with a people God loves and who love Him.
The section's أَجْر غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ is repeated for believers who do good, لَهُمْ أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ; the same wording makes reward's unbroken duration explicit.
The section's phrase أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ recurs for believers who do righteous deeds; its placement after the deniers' fate sharpens the lasting reward's contrast.
The section's dictionary root م ن ن links the wage that is not cut off; this ayah promises the Prophet a reward that is غير ممنون, using the same phrase.
The section's wage that survives life's cutoff meets the migrant who dies on the way: his reward has fallen to God's account, فَقَدْ وَقَعَ أَجْرُهُ عَلَى اللَّهِ.
The section's life ending and reward uncut meet those killed in God's path who are not dead but alive and provided for; death does not stop their life with God.
The section's wage continuing beyond bodily descent meets the rejoicing of those alive with their Lord over His bounty; this neighbor specifies their continuing provision.
The section's enduring wage meets the assurance that God does not waste believers' reward, لَا يُضِيعُ أَجْرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ; this completes the promise in 3:169–170.
The section's reward beyond life's end meets the people of Paradise praising God for removing sorrow; this neighbor leads to the next verse's explicit statement that fatigue no longer touches them.
The section's unexhausted wage meets the secure home where no weariness touches its people; this neighboring verse completes the contrast with the traveler's exhaustion.
The section's exhausted traveler and life's labor meet the address to humanity: you toil toward your Lord and will meet Him, كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ كَدْحًا.
The section's expiring life and wages that do not expire meet humanity being in loss, إِنَّ الْإِنسَانَ لَفِي خُسْرٍ; the next ayah names the exception.
The section's believers, sound deeds, and exclusion from descent meet those exempted from loss by faith, righteous work, truth, and patience.
The section's meeting of uprightness and crookedness in أَجْر is echoed by revelation with no عِوَج; this verse starts a passage that joins a straight book to lasting reward.
The section's q-w-m root for uprightness meets the Qur'an called قَيِّمًا, then good news for believers who do righteous deeds and receive a good wage.
The section's wage that does not end meets believers remaining in their reward forever, مَاكِثِينَ فِيهِ أَبَدًا; this completes the same passage's promise.
The section's straight stature and lasting reward meet those who say God is their Lord and then remain steadfast, اسْتَقَامُوا; the angels promise them the Garden.
The section's uprightness that holds through time meets those who affirm God as Lord and remain steadfast; the verse promises them freedom from fear and grief.
The section's wage that outlasts bodily life meets people preferring the nearer life, الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا; this verse names the choice opposed by enduring reward.
The section's uncut wage meets the declaration that the Hereafter is better and more enduring, وَالْآخِرَةُ خَيْرٌ وَأَبْقَىٰ; it states why the nearer life is not final.
The section's return and judgment oppose those who claim only worldly life and deny that anything destroys them but time; this ayah gives the exact denial the image answers.
The section's life, death, and return meet God's statement that He gives life and causes death and will gather people for the Day of Resurrection.
The section's الْبَلَدِ الْأَمِينِ meets the sanctuary made a place of return and safety, مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمْنًا; the place is both refuge and center.
The section's secure town joins safety to provision; Abraham asks for a town that is safe, بَلَدًا آمِنًا, and for its people to receive fruits.
The section's safe town is repeated in Abraham's prayer for Mecca, رَبِّ اجْعَلْ هَٰذَا الْبَلَدَ آمِنًا; the prayer protects the place where he settles his family.
The section's safe place as ground for human life meets Abraham's settlement in a barren valley and prayer that hearts incline and fruits be provided; this neighbor completes the provision scene.
The section's secure, provision-bearing town has its reversal here: a secure, tranquil town rejects its blessing and is clothed with hunger and fear, لِبَاسَ الْجُوعِ وَالْخَوْفِ.
The section's secure sanctuary meets the command to worship the Lord of this House; the next verse explains the concrete gifts attached to that place.
The section's safe town joins security with sustenance; God feeds its people against hunger and secures them from fear, أَطْعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعٍ وَآمَنَهُم مِّنْ خَوْفٍ.
The section's safe town meets the protected sanctuary whose people remain secure while people around them are seized; the ayah makes the safety geographical and precarious.
The section's secure town and provision meet the promise that believing, God-fearing towns would receive blessings from heaven and earth, بَرَكَاتٍ مِّنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ.
The section's safe town's reversal meets the question whether people of towns feel secure at night; the ayah makes apparent security the subject of warning.
The section's safety and provision meet the parallel warning about towns struck at forenoon while playing; this neighboring verse completes the reversal begun at 7:97.
The section's güvenli place meets people carving secure homes in mountains, آمِنِينَ; the next verse overturns their confidence.
The section's descent from a safe town meets the sudden blast that seizes those who thought themselves secure; this neighbor supplies the reversal to 15:82.
The section's oath by the secure town meets another oath by this town, هَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ; the next verses move from place and family to human creation.
The section's place as a setting for human life meets the address to the Prophet in this town; this neighbor continues the oath before parent and child.
The section places the town oath beside human formation; this neighbor adds parent and child, وَوَالِدٍ وَمَا وَلَدَ, before the claim about human toil.
The section's bodily formation and exhausted traveler meet the statement that humanity was created in hardship, فِي كَبَدٍ; the town oath and human condition meet in one surah.
The section's dictionary family for بَلَد includes earth and soil; this ayah sends rain to a dead land and says that is how the dead are brought forth.
The section's land/place image meets a dead town revived by rain, بَلَدٍ مَّيِّتٍ, followed by the explicit comparison to resurrection, كَذَٰلِكَ النُّشُورُ.
The section's town and ground meeting includes land that can collapse or revive; this ayah calls rain to a dead town and compares it with people being raised.
The section's town, soil, and provision converge in this ayah: a dead land is revived as provision for servants, and the resurrection is likened to that emergence.
The section's dictionary family for بَلَد joins a place to provision; this verse sends rain to revive a dead town and water people and livestock, without stating the resurrection comparison.
The section's Moses-at-the-Tur meeting begins when he sees a fire, آنَسَ مِن جَانِبِ الطُّورِ نَارًا; the following verse's encounter continues into fear and reassurance.
The section's fire scene becomes a divine call from the blessed side of the valley; this neighboring verse locates the encounter before 28:31 tells Moses not to fear.
The section connects Moses' fear at the fire to safety; God tells him not to fear and calls him among the secure, مِنَ الْآمِنِينَ, directly linking fear and trust.
The section's Moses-and-fire scene recurs as Moses sees a fire and hopes to bring news or a burning brand; the next verses turn the scene to divine reassurance.
The section's fire encounter is located in a blessed presence, with blessing on whoever is in or around it; this neighbor leads into the explicit reassurance at 27:9–10.
The section's fear-to-security movement at the Tur meets God's command not to fear in His presence; the staff scene turns fright into a protected encounter.
The section's fire seen during Moses' journey is repeated as he notices a fire and hopes to bring a brand; this verse begins the neighboring call at 20:11–12.
The section's fire scene continues when Moses reaches it and is called; the next verse identifies the sacred place, setting up the encounter's authority.
The section's meeting at the Tur becomes an instruction at the sacred valley; this neighbor completes the scene's setting, though it does not itself name the later fear.
The section's dictionary sense of أَمِين is dependable custody; Egypt's ruler calls Joseph trusted, أَمِينٌ, just as Joseph is appointed to guard provisions.
The section's reliable beast and secure place meet Joseph asking to oversee the land's storehouses as a knowledgeable keeper; this neighbor explains the work attached to his trust.
The section's dictionary form أَمِين names a dependable bearer; this verse values believers who keep trusts and covenants, وَالَّذِينَ هُمْ لِأَمَانَاتِهِمْ وَعَهْدِهِمْ رَاعُونَ.
The section's root أ م ن joins security and dependability; this repeated Qur'anic description praises those who guard trusts and covenants, here among the traits of the praying steadfast.
The section's dictionary sense of أَمُون is a dependable camel; this ayah directly invites readers to look at camels, الْإِبِلِ, and how they were created.

The section's dependable camel, exhausted traveler, and destination town converge in animals carrying heavy loads to a far country reachable only with great hardship, تَحْمِلُ أَثْقَالَكُمْ إِلَىٰ بَلَدٍ.

The section's dictionary family for بَلَد includes a camel's side falling to earth; here sacrificial camels stand and then their sides fall, فَإِذَا وَجَبَتْ جُنُوبُهَا, before people eat and feed others.
The section's word أَحْكَم joins securing workmanship against spoilage with judgment; this ayah uses the same root for a Book whose verses were made firm, أُحْكِمَتْ آيَاتُهُ.
The section contrasts God's true creation with human fabrication; Abraham asks about worshipping what people carve, مَا تَنْحِتُونَ, making human craft the scene's concrete example.
The section says the root خ ل ق separates God's creation from human making; this neighboring ayah says God created both people and what they do, وَاللَّهُ خَلَقَكُمْ وَمَا تَعْمَلُونَ.
The section's Moses-at-the-Tur scene includes fear at a transformed form; this ayah shows the staff becoming a moving serpent, the startling event answered by reassurance in the next verse.
The section's fear-to-safety meeting and return of a thing to its former state meet God's command to take the staff without fear and His promise to restore it, سَنُعِيدُهَا سِيرَتَهَا الْأُولَىٰ.
The section's well-proportioned human meets God's announcement that He will create a human from sounding clay; this verse begins the explicit formation scene.
The section's straightened body meets the completion of that creation when God has proportioned the human and breathed of His spirit, سَوَّيْتُهُ; this neighbor names the bodily act behind taqwim.
The section's best-formed human meets the repeated announcement of a human created from clay; this is a second Qur'anic telling of the formation scene.
The section's fashioned body meets the continuation in which God proportions the human and breathes of His spirit; this neighboring retelling confirms the same creation-to-form sequence.
The section's creation, return, and denial of dīn meet the question whether people thought they were created without purpose and would not be returned to God.
The section's sound deeds and uncut reward meet the lasting righteous deeds, الْبَاقِيَاتُ الصَّالِحَاتُ, said to be better in reward and hope than transient wealth and children.

The section asks what can still make a person deny the Recompense after creation and return; this ayah asks whether a human thinks he will be left without purpose, أَيَحْسَبُ الْإِنسَانُ أَن يُتْرَكَ سُدًى.
The section's outwardly measured deed and inwardly sound work meet the distinction that neither meat nor blood reaches God, but piety does; this neighbor explains what the sacrifice means.

The section's bodily descent and lasting wage meet worldly life pictured as rain-grown plants that dry into windblown debris, هَشِيمًا تَذْرُوهُ الرِّيَاحُ; the next verse names what remains valuable.
The section's exhausted traveler and mortal life meet the denial that the Creator was wearied by the first creation; the verse contrasts human fatigue with God's power to create anew.
The section's fatigued traveler and return from bodily decline meet the question whether the Creator, who made heaven and earth without weariness, can revive the dead.
The section brings a well-formed human into a meeting with height and place; after the camel, this neighboring ayah asks readers to consider how heaven was raised.
The section's straight, measured forms meet the next object in the same contemplation: mountains set firmly in place; this ayah continues the camel-and-creation scene.
The section's safe town and earth-bound descent meet the final object in the contemplation, the earth spread out; this verse completes the sequence begun with the camel.

The section's reliable camel meets the Qur'anic account of livestock created for human benefit, including warmth and food; it supplies the practical setting for the carrying animals in the next verses.
The section's sturdy animal and provision meet the beauty people find in bringing livestock home and taking them out to pasture; this neighbor continues the same animal scene.
The section's travel and load-bearing animal meet horses, mules, and donkeys provided for riding and adornment; this neighbor extends the journey scene beyond camels.
The section's root ح ك م includes making something firm; this ayah distinguishes firmly established verses, مُحْكَمَاتٌ, from ambiguous ones, a textual instance of that quality.
The section links upright human form with the root ق و م and dīn; this ayah names Abraham's straight path and a correct religion, دِينًا قِيَمًا.
The section's uprightness and just judgment meet the statement that judgment belongs to God and this is the correct religion, الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ; it joins both senses of the section's root.

The section's dictionary sense of م ن ن includes a cut rope, while this ayah tells believers to hold together to God's rope, حَبْلِ اللَّهِ, and not split apart; it offers a specific image of a bond kept intact.
The section's fire encounter turns fear toward safety; at this point in the same scene the voice identifies itself as God, grounding the following command not to fear.
The section's return to the just Judge meets the declaration that God is the true King and Lord of the noble Throne; this neighbor completes the answer to the claim of purposeless creation.
The section's formed human and return through bodily stages meet creation in the womb, خَلْقًا مِّن بَعْدِ خَلْقٍ; this ayah adds the hidden stages before birth.
The section's well-formed body meets human emergence from the mothers' wombs without knowledge, then hearing, sight, and hearts given by God; the verse makes bodily capacity a provision.
